knowledge_point_title: Writing a Linear System of Differential Equations in Matrix Form

canonical.:question/problem:
If the following system of differential equations is written in the form $\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),$ then what is the matrix $A?$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)+3{x}_{1}(t)-4{x}_{2}(t) &=0 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)-\sqrt{2}{x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t) &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
A first-order linear system of differential equations with two dependent variables is a system of equations that takes the following standard form:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) &=a(t){x}_{1}(t)+b(t){x}_{2}(t)+f(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) &=c(t){x}_{1}(t)+d(t){x}_{2}(t)+g(t)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where

- $a(t),$ $b(t),$ $c(t),$ $d(t),$ $f(t),$ and $g(t)$ are known functions, and

- $x_1(t)$ and $x_2(t)$ are unknown functions (dependent variables). 
Such a system can always be written in the form

$$
\mathbf x'(t) = A\mathbf x(t) + \mathbf f(t)
$$

where

$$
\mathbf x(t) = 
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{bmatrix},
\quad
A = 
\begin{bmatrix}a(t) & b(t) \\ c(t) & d(t)\end{bmatrix},
\quad
\mathbf f(t) = 
\begin{bmatrix}f(t) \\ g(t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We have the following system.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)+3{x}_{1}(t)-4{x}_{2}(t) &=0 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)-\sqrt{2}{x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t) &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Writing our system in standard form, we get the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) &=-3{x}_{1}(t)+4{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) &=\sqrt{2}{x}_{1}(t)-2{x}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we can rewrite our system in matrix form as follows:

$$
\mathbf x'(t) = 
\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 4 \\ \sqrt{2} & -2\end{bmatrix} \mathbf x(t)
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
A=
	\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 4 \\ \sqrt{2} & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

knowledge_point_title: Computing the Value of a Function of a Diagonal Matrix

canonical.:question/worked-solution:
Given a function $f$ and a diagonal matrix $D$ with diagonal entries $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n,$ we have
$$
f(D) = {\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}f ( {\lambda }_{1} ) & \cdots  & 0 \\ \vdots  & \ddots  & \vdots  \\ 0 & \cdots  & f ( {\lambda }_{n} )\end{array} \right]}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{log}⁡D & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{log}⁡(100) & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \operatorname{log}⁡(1) & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \operatorname{log}⁡(10)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
f(D)=\begin{bmatrix}f({\lambda }_{1}) & ⋯ & 0 \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & f({\lambda }_{n})\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{D} & =\begin{bmatrix}{2}^{3} & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{-2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}8 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{4}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical.:question/problem:
Given the function 
$f(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{w}) = w_1x_1^{3} + w_2x_2^{3},$
compute $\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} \: f$ with the input $\mathbf{x} = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}3 , \hspace{0.222em} - 2\end{array} \right]}^T.$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
To compute $\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} \: f$, we take partial derivatives with respect to each component of $\mathbf{w}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{w}_{1}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{w}_{1}}({w}_{1}{x}_{1}^{3}+{w}_{2}{x}_{2}^{3})={x}_{1}^{3} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂{w}_{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{w}_{2}}({w}_{1}{x}_{1}^{3}+{w}_{2}{x}_{2}^{3})={x}_{2}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, with $\mathbf{x} = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}3 , \hspace{0.222em} - 2\end{array} \right]}^T,$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{w}\,f & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}^{3} \\ {x}_{2}^{3}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}27 \\ -8\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$
